claim: Sleep alteration is a hallmark of ageing.
source: Sleep alteration is a hallmark of ageing and emerges as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and introduction, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: Sleep alteration emerges as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Sleep alteration is a hallmark of ageing and emerges as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: Earlier occurrence of spindles on slow-depolarisation SW is associated with higher medial prefrontal cortex Aβ burden (p=0.014, r²β*=0.06).
source: We found that, in contrast to other sleep metrics, earlier occurrence of spindles on slow-depolarisation SW is associated with higher medial prefrontal cortex Aβ burden (p=0.014, r²β*=0.06)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from the study, with specific p-value and effect size reported.

claim: Earlier occurrence of spindles on slow-depolarisation SW is predictive of greater longitudinal memory decline (p=0.032, r²β*=0.07, N=66).
source: earlier occurrence of spindles on slow-depolarisation SW is associated with higher medial prefrontal cortex Aβ burden (p=0.014, r²β*=0.06) and is predictive of greater longitudinal memory decline in a large subsample (p=0.032, r²β*=0.07, N=66).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal statistical analysis of experimental data from the study, with specific p-value, effect size, and sample size reported.

claim: Altered coupling of sleep microstructure elements contributes to poorer brain and cognitive trajectories in ageing.
source: These findings unravel early links between sleep, AD-related processes, and cognition and suggest that altered coupling of sleep microstructure elements, key to its mnesic function, contributes to poorer brain and cognitive trajectories in ageing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings about spindle-SW coupling and its associations with Aβ burden and memory decline.

claim: Sleep quality alterations are typical of the ageing process with more fragmented and less intense sleep detected as early as the fifth decade of life.
source: Alterations in sleep quality are typical of the ageing process with a more fragmented and less intense (or shallower) sleep detected as early as the fifth decade of life (Carrier et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Carrier et al., 2011).

claim: Alterations in sleep are predictive of the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease over the next 5–10 years.
source: Beyond healthy ageing, alterations in sleep are predictive of the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease (AD) over the next 5–10 years (Lim et al., 2013; Musiek and Holtzman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Lim et al., 2013; Musiek and Holtzman, 2016).

claim: Sleep disorders such as insomnia and obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome are associated with increased odds for AD diagnosis.
source: Similarly, sleep disorders such as insomnia and obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome are associated with increased odds for AD diagnosis (Baril et al., 2018; Elias et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Baril et al., 2018; Elias et al., 2018).

claim: Brain burdens of aggregated amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau proteins have been linked with reduced sleep intensity in healthy and cognitively normal older individuals aged >70 years.
source: Brain burdens of aggregated amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau proteins, hallmarks of AD pathophysiology, have been linked with a reduced sleep intensity, as indexed by the overall production of slow waves (SW) during sleep, but also to worse objective sleep efficiency and subjective sleep quality, in healthy and cognitively normal older individuals aged >70 years (Mander et al., 2015; Ju et al., 2017; Lucey et al., 2019; Kang et al., 2009; Ju et al., 2013; Sprecher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Experimental sleep deprivation and sleep fragmentation lead to increased concentration of Aβ in the CSF in animal models and healthy human populations.
source: Sleep alteration may, in turn, contribute to the aggregation of Aβ and tau proteins: experimental sleep deprivation and sleep fragmentation (disturbance in the production of SW during sleep) lead to increased concentration of Aβ in the CSF, both in animal models and in healthy human populations (Ju et al., 2017; Kang et al., 2009; Lucey et al., 2018; Ooms et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Ju et al., 2017; Kang et al., 2009; Lucey et al., 2018; Ooms et al., 2014).

claim: A bidirectional detrimental relationship between sleep quality and the neuropathology of AD is emerging in the literature.
source: Overall, a bidirectional detrimental relationship between sleep quality and the neuropathology of AD is emerging in the literature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about the relationships between sleep and AD pathology.

claim: Sleep may constitute a modifiable risk factor which one could act upon to prevent or delay the neuropathological processes associated to AD.
source: Sleep may therefore constitute a modifiable risk factor which one could act upon to prevent or delay the neuropathological processes associated to AD and favour successful cognitive trajectories over the lifespan (Van Egroo et al., 2019b; Ju et al., 2014; Wang and Holtzman, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential interventions, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sleep is not yet widely recognised as an independent risk factor for AD.
source: Hitherto, however, sleep is not yet widely recognised as an independent risk factor for AD, and the mechanistic associations between sleep and early AD neuropathology are not yet fully established.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific consensus.

claim: The mechanistic associations between sleep and early AD neuropathology are not yet fully established.
source: Hitherto, however, sleep is not yet widely recognised as an independent risk factor for AD, and the mechanistic associations between sleep and early AD neuropathology are not yet fully established.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Higher density of both sleep spindles and slow waves during post-learning sleep has been linked to better overnight memory consolidation.
source: Sleep microstructure elements, such as sleep spindles and SW, are essential correlates of the cognitive functions of sleep, as higher density of both elements during post-learning sleep has been linked to a better overnight memory consolidation (Ulrich, 2016; Gais et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2006; Mednick et al., 2013; Miyamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The slower portion of SW activity was reported to modulate the regression between the burden of Aβ over the prefrontal cortex and lower overnight memory consolidation in cognitively normal older individuals.
source: Furthermore, the slower portion of SW activity (i.e. a power measure combining the density and amplitude of sleep SW over sleep cycles in the 0.6–1 Hz band) was reported to modulate the regression between the burden of Aβ over the prefrontal cortex and a lower overnight memory consolidation in cognitively normal older individuals (Mander et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Mander et al., 2015).

claim: The fine-tuned coupling of spindles and SW has been reported to be altered in ageing, with an earlier occurrence of the spindle relative to the SW depolarisation phase in older compared to younger individuals.
source: The fine-tuned coupling of spindles and SW has further been reported to be altered in ageing, with an earlier occurrence of the spindle relative to the SW depolarisation phase in the older compared to younger individuals, and to predict overnight memory retention (Helfrich et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Helfrich et al., 2018).

claim: Altered spindle-SW coupling predicts overnight memory retention.
source: The fine-tuned coupling of spindles and SW has further been reported to be altered in ageing, with an earlier occurrence of the spindle relative to the SW depolarisation phase in the older compared to younger individuals, and to predict overnight memory retention (Helfrich et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Helfrich et al., 2018).

claim: A study in 31 individuals aged around 75 years found a link between the brain deposit of tau protein and the coupling of spindles and SW.
source: A study in 31 individuals, aged around 75 years, found a link between the brain deposit of tau protein and the coupling of spindles and SW (Winer, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Winer, 2019).

claim: Another research failed to find a link between spindle-SW coupling and Aβ brain burden.
source: By contrast, another research failed to find a link between this coupling and Aβ brain burden (Winer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Winer et al., 2020).

claim: The difficulty to detect the link between spindle-SW coupling and Aβ burden may be due to assessments being carried out late over the lifespan (>70 years), when subtle associations may be masked by concurrent brain alterations.
source: Here, we argue that, on top of potential statistical power issues, the difficulty to detect this link may be due to the fact that the assessments were carried out late over the lifespan (i.e. >70 years), when subtle associations may be masked by concurrent brain alterations, and by the heterogeneity of sleep SW.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation by the authors about why previous studies may have failed to detect associations.

claim: The low frequency oscillations of the EEG during NREM sleep have been divided into slow oscillations (≤1 Hz) and delta waves (1–4 Hz) for decades in humans.
source: The low frequency oscillations of the electroencephalography (EEG) during non-Rapid Eye Movement (NREM) sleep have been divided in slow oscillations (≤1 Hz) and delta waves (1–4 Hz) for decades in humans, notably based on the theoretical framework of the generation of SWs (Achermann and Borbély, 1997; Lee et al., 2004; Hubbard et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research establishing this classification.

claim: A recent work proposed the transition frequency of the down-to-up state as an objective way of distinguishing between slow and fast switcher SWs.
source: As one of the main features of the SW resides in their transition from down- to up-state, reflecting synchronised depolarisation, a recent work proposed the transition frequency of the down-to-up state as an objective way of distinguishing between slow and fast switcher SWs (Bouchard et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Bouchard et al., 2021).

claim: Older individuals exhibit higher probabilities of producing slow as compared to fast switcher SWs.
source: Compared to young adults, on top of exhibiting a typical overall lower density of SW, older individuals reportedly exhibit higher probabilities of producing slow as compared to fast switcher SWs, providing important insights into age-related changes in sleep microstructure.
evidence: This is stated as a reported finding from previous research, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Slow and fast switcher SWs constitute distinct realisations of NREM oscillations that are differently associated with brain aggregation of Aβ during the ageing process.
source: This finding reinforces the idea that slow and fast switcher SWs constitute distinct realisations of NREM oscillations that are differently associated with brain aggregation of Aβ during the ageing process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical findings about differential distributions and associations.

source: In fact, when testing the association between the coupling of spindles and SWs, irrespective of the type of SWs, and PET Aβ burden over the MPFC, the statistical analysis only yields a weak negative association between the phase of the coupling of the spindles onto the SWs and Aβ burden (main effect of Aβ uptake: F196=3.96, p=0.049, r²β*=0.04; main effect of sex: F196=4.33, p=0.04, r²β*=0.04; main effect of age: F1,96=0.05, p=0.83)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: The coupling of sleep microstructure elements matters rather than their individual occurrence.
source: This suggests a specific role for the coupling of both elements of sleep microstructure. Moreover and as previously reported in an intermediate analysis of a subsample of the same study (Van Egroo et al., 2019a), we do not find significant associations between more macroscopic measures, which are typically used to characterise sleep, and the accumulation of Aβ protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results showing coupling but not density associations.

claim: The density of SWs irrespective of their type was not associated with MPFC Aβ burden (F195=1.18, p=0.28).
source: Likewise, unlike previous reports (Mander et al., 2015; Winer, 2019), we did not find any association between the MPFC Aβ burden and the density of SWs, irrespective of their type (F195=1.18, p=0.28)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

source: in our sample, power in the 0.5–1 Hz EEG frequency band as well as the ratio between the power in the 0.5–1 Hz and 1–4 Hz bands were not associated with the burden of Aβ (main effect of Aβ burden: F195<2.85, p≥0.10)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: The ratio between the power in the 0.5–1 Hz and 1–4 Hz bands was not associated with the burden of Aβ (main effect of Aβ burden: F195<2.85, p≥0.10).
source: in our sample, power in the 0.5–1 Hz EEG frequency band as well as the ratio between the power in the 0.5–1 Hz and 1–4 Hz bands were not associated with the burden of Aβ (main effect of Aβ burden: F195<2.85, p≥0.10)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: A large subsample (N=66) completed a follow-up visit at 2 years which included the MST.
source: A large subsample (N=66) completed a follow-up visit at 2 years which included the MST consisting in a pattern separation task targeting the ability to distinguish between highly resembling memory events, a hippocampus-dependent task which is very sensitive to early cognitive decline (Stark et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct report of the study design and data collection.

claim: An overall decline in performance between the baseline and follow-up performance at the MST was observed (t65=2.19, p=0.032).
source: We first observed an overall decline in performance between the baseline and follow-up performance at the MST (t65=2.19, p=0.032).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: There is a significant negative link between the relative change in memory performance and the phase of spindle anchoring onto slow switcher SWs (main effect of spindle-slow switcher SW coupling: F161=4.80, p=0.032, r²β*=0.07).
source: Statistical analyses revealed a significant negative link between the relative change in memory performance and the phase of spindle anchoring onto slow switcher SWs, indicating that an earlier spindle onset is predictive of a memory worsening over 2 years (main effect of spindle-slow switcher SW coupling: F161=4.80, p=0.032, r²β*=0.07)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: An earlier spindle onset is predictive of memory worsening over 2 years.
source: Statistical analyses revealed a significant negative link between the relative change in memory performance and the phase of spindle anchoring onto slow switcher SWs, indicating that an earlier spindle onset is predictive of a memory worsening over 2 years (main effect of spindle-slow switcher SW coupling: F161=4.80, p=0.032, r²β*=0.07)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical finding about the direction of the association.

claim: No association was detected between spindle coupling to fast switcher SWs and memory performance change (main effect of spindle-fast switcher SW coupling: F161=2.51, p=0.12).
source: No such association was detected when considering spindle coupling to fast switcher SWs (main effect of spindle-fast switcher SW coupling: F161=2.51, p=0.12; main effect of age: F161=0.33, p=0.57; main effect of sex: F161=0.18, p=0.68; and main effect of education: F161=1.11, p=0.30).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: Memory performance change over 2 years was not significantly related to the MPFC Aβ burden (main effect of Aβ burden: F160=2.33, p=0.13).
source: Further statistical analyses show that the memory performance change over the 2 year was not significantly related to the MPFC Aβ burden (main effect of Aβ burden: F160=2.33, p=0.13; main effect of age: F160=1.27, p=0.26; main effect of sex: F160=0.03, p=0.87; and main effect of education: F160=0.41, p=0.53).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: There was no significant link between the coupling of the spindles onto both SW types and the baseline performance on the MST (main effect of spindle-SW coupling: F196≥0.2, p≤0.61).
source: When considering baseline performance to the MST across the entire sample (N=100; i.e. assessed at the same time as the sleep measures), we found no significant link between the coupling of the spindles onto both SW types and the performance on the task (main effect of spindle-SW coupling: F196≥0.2, p≤0.61; main effect of age: F196≤0.36, p≥0.55; main effect of sex: F196≤0.54, p≥0.46; and main effect of education: F196≤0.47, p≥0.50 (Figure 2b–c)).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: The results provide compelling evidence that the link between sleep and the accumulation of Aβ over the MPFC involves the precise and timely coupling of spindles and SWs.
source: Overall, our results provide compelling evidence that the link between sleep and the accumulation of Aβ over the MPFC, an early AD-related brain features, involves the precise and timely coupling of two key elements of NREM sleep, spindles and SWs, and that this coupling bears a predictive value for the subsequent decline in memory performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results showing associations between coupling and both Aβ burden and memory decline.

claim: Spindle-SW coupling bears a predictive value for the subsequent decline in memory performance.
source: Overall, our results provide compelling evidence that the link between sleep and the accumulation of Aβ over the MPFC, an early AD-related brain features, involves the precise and timely coupling of two key elements of NREM sleep, spindles and SWs, and that this coupling bears a predictive value for the subsequent decline in memory performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the longitudinal association between coupling and memory decline.

claim: The number of spindles or SWs generated overnight is not associated with the accumulation of Aβ over the MPFC in healthy and relatively young older adults.
source: Our study does not indicate, at least not in these healthy and relatively young older adults, that the number of spindles or SWs generated overnight is associated with the accumulation of Aβ over the MPFC.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the statistical analyses showing no associations between densities and Aβ burden.

claim: Sleep SWs provide a readout of the homeostatic sleep pressure and are more prevalent at the beginning relative to the end of the night.
source: Sleep SWs provide a readout of the homeostatic sleep pressure and are more prevalent at the beginning relative to the end of the night (Achermann et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Achermann et al., 1993).

claim: Both the density of spindles and SWs have separately been related to overnight consolidation of memory.
source: In addition, both the density of spindles and SWs have separately been related to overnight consolidation of memory (Miyamoto et al., 2017; Fernandez and Lüthi, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spindles and SWs actively take part in information transfer from hippocampic to neocortical networks and in synaptic plasticity.
source: They actively take part in information transfer from hippocampic to neocortical networks and in synaptic plasticity (Ulrich, 2016; Miyamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In younger individuals, spindles tend to reach their maximum around the cortical up-state of the SWs, whereas in older individuals, spindles occur earlier on the depolarisation phase of the SWs.
source: In the younger individuals, spindles tend to reach their maximum around the cortical up-state of the SWs, whereas in older individuals, spindles occur earlier on the depolarisation phase of the SWs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Earlier coupling between spindles and SWs is related to poorer overnight memory retention.
source: This earlier coupling between spindles and SWs is related to a poorer overnight memory retention (Helfrich et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Helfrich et al., 2018).

claim: Individuals for which the spindles occur earlier during the transition phase of the slow switcher SWs show higher Aβ burden over the MPFC and worse memory change over time.
source: In line with a presumed suboptimal coupling between spindles and SWs, we find that, when controlling for age, individuals for which the spindles occur earlier during the transition phase of the slow switcher SWs show higher Aβ burden over the MPFC and a worse memory change over time.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings from the statistical analyses.

claim: There was no significant effect of the age of participants on the phase of the coupling between spindles and SWs.
source: We did not find any significant effect of the age of participants on the phase of the coupling between spindles and SWs.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the study data.

claim: The lack of age effect on spindle-SW coupling is likely due to the restricted age range of participants and variability between individuals in sleep changes during ageing.
source: This is likely due, in part, to the restricted age range of our participants, but also to the variability existing between the individuals in the changes they undergo in their sleep during ageing.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about why they did not find an age effect.

claim: The relationship between the phase of the spindle onset onto the SWs and the MPFC Aβ burden shows the same directionality (earlier spindles onto SWs) as the changes previously reported in older individuals.
source: Importantly, the relationship we observed between the phase of the spindle onset onto the SWs and the MPFC Aβ burden shows the same directionality (i.e. earlier spindles onto SWs) as the changes previously reported in older individuals.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the study's findings to previous research.

claim: The slow switcher SWs were relatively preserved in older individuals compared to the fast switcher SWs.
source: Beyond the well-known decrease in the production of SWs in ageing, the slow switcher SWs were relatively preserved in the older individuals compared to the fast switcher SWs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous research.

claim: Sleep spindles occurring concomitantly to slow switchers SWs show a clear preference to the late part of the depolarisation phase.
source: While spindles occurring concomitantly to slow switchers SWs show a clear preference to the late part of the depolarisation phase, spindles co-occurring with fast switcher SWs show more widespread phase of coupling (that is still not randomly/uniformly distributed).
evidence: This is a description of the data pattern observed in the study.

claim: Spindles co-occurring with fast switcher SWs show more widespread phase of coupling.
source: While spindles occurring concomitantly to slow switchers SWs show a clear preference to the late part of the depolarisation phase, spindles co-occurring with fast switcher SWs show more widespread phase of coupling (that is still not randomly/uniformly distributed).
evidence: This is a description of the data pattern observed in the study.

claim: Only the coupling of spindles onto slow switcher SWs was significantly associated to the early accumulation of Aβ in the brain.
source: Furthermore, only the coupling of spindles onto slow switcher SWs was significantly associated to the early accumulation of Aβ in the brain.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical findings from the study.

claim: Only the coupling of spindles and slow switcher SWs was predictive of the memory change after 2 years.
source: Finally, only the coupling of spindles and slow switcher SWs was predictive of the memory change after 2 years.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical findings from the study.

claim: Slow switcher SWs are important to the development of AD-related pathological changes in the form of Aβ protein accumulation.
source: Our results support that slow switcher SWs, the type previously reported to be relatively spared during ageing (Bouchard et al., 2021), are important to the development of AD-related pathological changes, at least in the form of Aβ protein accumulation, and for the subsequent development of subtle alteration in cognitive abilities, leastways over the memory domain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of associations found in the study.

claim: Slow switcher SWs are important for the subsequent development of subtle alteration in cognitive abilities over the memory domain.
source: Our results support that slow switcher SWs, the type previously reported to be relatively spared during ageing (Bouchard et al., 2021), are important to the development of AD-related pathological changes, at least in the form of Aβ protein accumulation, and for the subsequent development of subtle alteration in cognitive abilities, leastways over the memory domain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of associations found in the study.

claim: Sleep spindles are considered as thalamic events generated through the interplay between the inhibitory reticular nucleus and the excitatory thalamocortical neurons.
source: Sleep spindles are considered as thalamic events. They are generated through the interplay between the inhibitory reticular nucleus and the excitatory thalamocortical neurons, which project to the cortical neurons that feedback in turns to the thalamus (Ulrich, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: SWs are intrinsically cortical and consist in the spontaneous alternations between down (hyperpolarised) and up (depolarised) neuronal states.
source: In contrast, SWs are intrinsically cortical. They consist in the spontaneous alternations between down (hyperpolarised) and up (depolarised) neuronal states (Adamantidis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The thalamus reticular nucleus contributes to the synchronisation of distant neuronal populations during SWs.
source: The SWs undergo, however, an influence from the thalamus reticular nucleus that contributes to the synchronisation of distant neuronal populations (Lee et al., 2004; Adamantidis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The thalamus reticular neurons could be involved in the functional associations between spindles and SWs.
source: Hence, although the exact neurophysiological origin of the functional associations between spindles and SWs remain to be established, the thalamus reticular neurons could arguably be involved.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the neurophysiological mechanisms.

claim: The early aggregation of Aβ protein in the MPFC could disturb the thalamocortical interplay, driving the coalescence of spindles and SWs.
source: Our results would therefore indicate that the early aggregation of Aβ protein in the MPFC could disturb the thalamocortical interplay, driving the coalescence of spindles and SWs.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the mechanistic interpretation of their findings.

claim: Chronic disturbance in spindle-SW coupling would trigger the cognitive changes detectable after 2 years.
source: This chronic disturbance would then trigger the cognitive changes detectable after 2 years.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the temporal sequence of events.

claim: The cross-sectional nature of the imaging data does not allow inferences regarding the directionality of the relationship between the spindle-slow switcher SW coupling and the burden of Aβ protein.
source: The cross-sectional nature of our imaging data does not, however, allow to make inferences regarding the directionality of the relationship between the spindle-slow switcher SW coupling and the burden of Aβ protein.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study design.

claim: Evidence accumulates to show that if AD-neuropathological hallmarks can affect the quality of sleep, sleep can also impinge onto these hallmarks.
source: Evidence accumulates to show that if AD-neuropathological hallmarks can affect the quality of sleep, sleep can also impinge onto these hallmarks (Van Egroo et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is stated as emerging evidence supported by a citation.

claim: The occurrence of the SWs has been associated with a transient increase in the glymphatic flow related to local variations in neuromodulator concentrations.
source: Specifically relevant in the context of this study, the occurrence of the SWs has been associated with a transient increase in the glymphatic flow related to local variations in neuromodulator concentrations (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Xie et al., 2013).

claim: It is possible that the changes in the density of SWs occurring during ageing affect both their coupling with spindles and the early accumulation of Aβ protein.
source: It is therefore possible that the changes in the density of SWs occurring during ageing affect both their coupling with spindles and the early accumulation of Aβ protein.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about potential mechanisms.

claim: The cumulated power of the oscillations generated over the entire 0.5–4 Hz delta band was not associated with PET measures.
source: The cumulated power of the oscillations generated over the entire 0.5–4 Hz delta band (i.e. the SWE) or only over the slower 0.5–1 Hz portion of SWE (as in Mander et al., 2015) as well as the ratio between slower (0.5–1 Hz) and faster (1–4 Hz) SWE (as in Mander et al., 2015) was not associated with PET measures.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical findings from the study.

claim: The alteration in the microstructure of sleep shows a prior association with AD-related processes compared with the amount of slow brain oscillations generated during overnight sleep.
source: Altogether, these discrepancies reinforce the idea that the alteration in the microstructure of sleep, consisting in the coupling of the spindles onto a specific subpopulation of SWs, as reported here, but also in the occurrence of microarousals during sleep we previously reported based on the same sample (Chylinski et al., 2021), shows a prior association with AD-related processes compared with the amount of slow brain oscillations generated during overnight sleep.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the current findings to previous research.

claim: The amount of slow brain oscillations may only be significantly associated with AD-related processes at a later age, when the pathophysiological changes are already more substantial.
source: The latter may only be significantly associated at a later age, when the pathophysiological changes are already more substantial.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about why their findings differ from previous research.

claim: The coupling of spindles onto slow switcher SWs is predictive of future-cognitive and brain-ageing trajectory.
source: In addition, the coupling of spindles onto slow switcher SWs is predictive of the future change in memory performance. Sleep microstructure could therefore constitute a promising early marker of future-cognitive and brain-ageing trajectory (Chylinski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the longitudinal findings of the study.

claim: Sleep microstructure could constitute a promising early marker of future-cognitive and brain-ageing trajectory.
source: Sleep microstructure could therefore constitute a promising early marker of future-cognitive and brain-ageing trajectory (Chylinski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation about the potential clinical utility of the findings.

claim: Fast spindles are rather coupled to the up-state of the SWs and slow spindles tend to occur on the waning depolarisation phase of the SWs.
source: As some reports describe that fast spindles are rather coupled to the up-state of the SWs and slow spindles tend to occur on the waning depolarisation phase of the SWs (Mölle et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Mölle et al., 2011).

claim: The associations observed are probably rather driven by fast spindles.
source: we could hypothesise that the associations we observe are probably rather driven by fast spindles.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about which spindle types drive the observed associations.

claim: The study may have insufficient power to detect some associations with other sleep measures.
source: First, although we collected data in a relatively large sample, we may have insufficient power to detect some associations with other sleep measures.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Association between spindle-SWs coupling and the early accumulation of Aβ protein is at least stronger than the association with other sleep measures.
source: One can nevertheless frame our findings in relative terms such that association between spindle-SWs coupling and the early accumulation of Aβ protein is at least stronger than the association with the coupling of spindles onto fast switchers SW, the density of SWs and spindles, the SWE, etc.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing effect sizes across different analyses.

claim: Effect sizes of the significant associations found were relatively small, in line with the complex and multifactorial nature of AD.
source: Also, effect sizes of the significant associations we found were relatively small, in line with the complex and multifactorial nature of AD.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the effect sizes in the context of AD complexity.

claim: The longitudinal aspect of the study is relatively short-termed and only concerned the performance to a sensitive mnesic task.
source: In addition, the longitudinal aspect of our study is relatively short-termed and only concerned the performance to a sensitive mnesic task while it did not include sleep EEG and the PET assessments.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study design.

claim: The protocol does not include manipulation of the coupling of the spindles onto the SWs, precluding any inference on causality.
source: Finally, given that our protocol does not include manipulation of the coupling of the spindles onto the SWs, it precludes any inference on the causality of one aspect onto the other.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study design.

claim: Cognition and the coupling of spindles and SWs may be sensitive to the same age-related or AD-related phenomenon.
source: It may be that cognition and the coupling of spindles and SWs are sensitive to the same age-related or AD-related phenomenon (e.g. presence of amyloid oligomers, or non-amyloid processes, that would go mostly undetected using common PET scan Aβ radioligand; Yamin and Teplow, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about alternative explanations for the associations.

claim: The timely occurrence of spindles onto slow switcher SWs may play an important role in ageing trajectory, both at the cognitive level and with regards to structural brain integrity.
source: Together, our findings reveal that the timely occurrence of spindles onto a specific type of SWs showing a relative preservation in ageing may play an important role in ageing trajectory, both at the cognitive level and with regards to structural brain integrity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of findings in the study.

claim: These findings may help to unravel early links between sleep, AD-related pathophysiology, and cognitive trajectories in ageing.
source: These findings may help to unravel early links between sleep, AD-related pathophysiology, and cognitive trajectories in ageing and warrants future clinical trials attempting at manipulating sleep microstructure or Aβ protein accumulation.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: The findings warrant future clinical trials attempting at manipulating sleep microstructure or Aβ protein accumulation.
source: These findings may help to unravel early links between sleep, AD-related pathophysiology, and cognitive trajectories in ageing and warrants future clinical trials attempting at manipulating sleep microstructure or Aβ protein accumulation.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions based on the findings.

claim: 101 healthy participants aged from 50 to 70 years (68 women; mean ± SD = 59.4±5.3 years) were enrolled between 15 June 2016 and 2 October 2019.
source: 101 healthy participants aged from 50 to 70 years (68 women; mean ± SD = 59.4±5.3 years) were enrolled between 15 June 2016 and 2 October 2019 for a multimodal cross-sectional study taking place at the GIGA-Cyclotron Research Centre/In Vivo Imaging of the University of Liège (Cognitive fitness in ageing – COFITAGE – study) which has already led to several scientific publications (e.g. Chylinski et al., 2021; Rizzolo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct report of the study design and participant characteristics.

claim: One participant was excluded from analyses due to the lack of PET imaging data.
source: One participant was excluded from analyses due to the lack of PET imaging data.
evidence: This is a direct report of the study sample.

claim: Only the frontal electrodes were considered because the frontal cortex is an early site showing Aβ deposit and is the primary generator of the SWs during sleep.
source: Only the frontal electrodes were considered because the frontal cortex is an early site showing Aβ deposit and is the primary generator of the SWs during sleep (Mander et al., 2015; Dang-Vu et al., 2005; Dang-Vu et al., 2010; Saletin et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a methodological decision justified by citations to previous research.

claim: Aβ PET imaging was performed using [18F] Flutemetamol, except for three volunteers for which [18F] Florbetapir was used.
source: Aβ PET imaging was performed using [18F] Flutemetamol, except for three volunteers for which [18F] Florbetapir was used.
evidence: This is a direct report of the study methods.

claim: SUVR values were converted into Centiloid units.
source: As images were acquired using two different radioligands, their SUVR values were converted into Centiloid units (Klunk et al., 2015) (the validation of the procedure in our sample was previously published Narbutas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct report of the study methods, supported by citations.

claim: The Aβ burden was averaged over a mask covering the MPFC, previously reported to undergo the earliest aggregation sites for Aβ pathology.
source: The Aβ burden was averaged over a mask covering the MPFC, previously reported to undergo the earliest aggregation sites for Aβ pathology (Grothe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological decision justified by a citation to previous research.

claim: The MST is a hippocampus-dependent task which is very sensitive to early cognitive decline.
source: A large subsample (N=66) completed a follow-up visit at 2 years which included the MST consisting in a pattern separation task targeting the ability to distinguish between highly resembling memory events, a hippocampus-dependent task which is very sensitive to early cognitive decline (Stark et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Stark et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2017).

claim: The second neuropsychological evaluation was carried out ~24 months after the first one (mean 767±54 days).
source: The second neuropsychological evaluation was carried out ~24 months after the first one (mean 767±54 days)
evidence: This is a direct report of the study design.

claim: The study was registered with EudraCT 2016-001436-35.
source: The study was registered with EudraCT 2016-001436-35.
evidence: This is a direct report of the study registration.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Hospital-Faculty Ethics Committee of ULiège.
source: All procedures were approved by the Hospital-Faculty Ethics Committee of ULiège.
evidence: This is a direct report of ethical approval.
